feature.name: Pricing Change
feature.description:
current pricing tiers are 0$(limited use case) and 20$(full access)
which we are not changing to 20$(full access with limits on total discounts) and 50$(full access + no limits)

verdictRationale: finalVerdict is iterate, directly aligned with the personaFleet recommendation of iterate and consistent with financial's proceed_with_caution. The fleet evidence shows the $20 cap is a churn vector and the $50 tier polarizes, so shipping as-is is not supported; the low-cost, one-week profile means a revised-cap test (not a stop) is the right next step.
executiveSummary: Fly Upsell & Cross Sell's proposed pricing change ($20 capped / $50 unlimited) is a low-cost, one-week experiment within the $10k threshold, backed by 18-month runway and $0 burn. However, evidence is polarized: the $20 discount cap reads as a downgrade/repackaging, satisfaction is low (mean 31.4), and low-volume/stable merchants reject the $50 tier. The $50 unlimited plan resonates with high-volume BFCM and promotional merchants (upgrade means 90.4 and 88.3). Regression is skipped with no payload. Persona fleet recommends iterate; financial recommends proceed with caution. Executive decision: iterate—revise the $20 cap, add usage transparency, and test with merchant cohorts before broad rollout.

market.summary: Market scan is available but thin. Competitor published bundle/AOV pricing clusters roughly $15–$60/month (Kaching $14.99/$29.99/$59.99; Shopify blog Nov 4, 2024 cites Kaching paid plans from ~$15 Starter to ~$30 Scale plus Pro). Rapi Bundles' Pro plan is documented as covering up to $10,000 of extra usage, an existing usage-capped pattern. The new $50 tier sits at the top of the observed band; the recapped $20 sits near competitor entry pricing (~$15). BFCM capacity is an explicit category marketing theme. Internal ARPU is $8/merchant/month with $9k MRR, implying ~1,125 merchants; retention is 4 months and average LTV is $40 vs $4 CAC. Competitor enrichment and job-market queries failed, and no internal upgrade, churn, or discount-usage data were provided.
highlights: Competitor list prices cluster roughly $15–$60/month; the new $50 tier lands at the top of the observed band.
Usage-capped monetization already exists among direct competitors (Rapi Pro plan covers up to $10,000 of extra usage).
Peak-season (BFCM) capacity is an explicit marketing battleground in the category.
The category is crowded, with Rebolt citing 10K+ merchants, Simple Bundles 15,000+ stores, and BundleSuite 2,000+ brands.
Merchants are openly price-sensitive, per a surfaced Reddit thread on bundle/quantity-break app pricing.
Current ARPU is far below competitor list prices: $8 revenue per merchant per month vs competitor entry prices from $14.99–$15/month.
risks: The change reduces what existing $20 customers receive at the same price by introducing discount limits, creating churn and downgrade risk.
Competitor entry prices are lower, so merchants who hit the new cap may substitute rather than upgrade to $50.
Retention is only 4 months with average LTV of $40 against a CAC of $4; pricing friction burns through that payback window quickly.
Category crowding makes a 150% top-tier price increase easy to benchmark and easy to leave.
Competitor intelligence is unverified: company_enrich calls for Rapi Bundles, Fast Bundles, and Kaching Bundles failed.
No job-market signal was obtained; both job_search calls errored.
Support impact is an assumption: 20% support occupancy is stated without a ticket-volume or pricing-query baseline.

The $10,000 financialThresholdAmount has no stated definition; if read as monthly incremental revenue, at $30 per upgrade it implies roughly 334 upgrades (derived), approximately 30% of the implied 1,125 merchant base.
Delivery is sized at one engineer at 20% occupancy over one week, a compressed window for pricing, entitlement enforcement, billing display, and support documentation.

personaFleet.summary: Persona fleet recommendation is iterate. Composite mean 46.5, median 48.6, percentLikelyAdopt 0. The $50 unlimited tier strongly appeals to high-volume BFCM/promotional personas (upgrade means 90.4 and 88.3; importance of unlimited discounts near-max at 96.4 and 94.3). But the capped $20 tier is widely seen as a downgrade/repackaging: satisfaction with new pricing is low (mean 31.4), recommendation likelihood is 43.1 with no scores in the 80–100 range, and low-volume/stable personas reject the $50 tier (upgrade means 8.8 and 11.3). The response is structurally polarized.
highlights: Fleet composite mean 46.5, median 48.6, percentLikelyAdopt 0.
$50 unlimited tier upgrade means: 90.4 for persona_1 and 88.3 for persona_2.
Importance of unlimited discounts: 96.4 for persona_1 and 94.3 for persona_2.
$20 capped plan continuation means: 86.2 for persona_3 and 73.2 for new_install.
Satisfaction with new pricing mean 31.4; 20 of 25 agents scored in the 20–39 range.
Recommendation likelihood mean 43.1 with no scores in the 80–100 range.
Polarized upgrade intent: 12 agents scored 0–19 and 13 scored 80–100 on upgradeToFiftyForUnlimited.

financial.summary: Financial status is available. Investment threshold is $10k, duration 1 week, with 1 engineer at 20% occupancy and support at 20% occupancy. CFO verdict is within_threshold. Company health: $9k MRR, 70% margins, $0 burn, 18 months runway, $8 revenue per merchant per month, $4 CAC, 4-month retention, and $40 average LTV. Financial recommendation is proceed_with_caution, driven by polarized market feedback: the $20 cap reads as a downgrade, while high-volume merchants show strong $50 upgrade intent. CFO workspace calls returned validation errors; only an uploaded report reference is available.
highlights: One-week effort with 1 engineer at 20% occupancy and support at 20% occupancy is within the $10k threshold.
Runway is 18 months with $9k MRR, 70% margins, and $0 burn.
The $50 unlimited tier is compelling for high-volume BFCM and promotional merchants.
High-upgrade-intent personas show strong interest in unlimited discounts.
The change is low-cost and short-duration, making it easy to test before broad rollout.
Positive margins, $0 burn, and 18 months of runway provide capacity for a measured pricing experiment.

crossCuttingThemes: The $20 discount cap is widely perceived as a downgrade or repackaging of prior full access, creating churn and downgrade risk.
The $50 unlimited tier has strong fit with high-volume BFCM/promotional merchants but is rejected by low-volume and stable merchants.
The response is structurally polarized, so averages mask opposing merchant reactions.
The change is low-cost and short-duration, testable within the $10k threshold and supported by 18 months of runway.
Support load is assumed at 20% occupancy but lacks a ticket-volume or pricing-query baseline.
Competitor intelligence and internal upgrade/churn/discount-usage data are incomplete.
BFCM/peak-season timing is a shared opportunity across market and persona evidence.
conditions: Revise or grandfather the $20 discount cap so existing full-access merchants do not experience a same-price downgrade.
Add an in-app discount-usage meter with a clear upgrade path to the $50 unlimited tier.
Stage rollout to BFCM/promotional high-volume merchants first; hold broad rollout until cap messaging is validated.
Validate pricing and cap thresholds with merchant cohorts before launch.
Provide self-serve pricing documentation and support playbooks to manage expected pricing queries.
Monitor support load, churn, downgrade rate, and $20→$50 conversion by merchant cohort.
Re-run regression testing on billing display, entitlement enforcement, and discount-limit logic before any launch.
